newsitem.title: UK: British manufacturing shows fresh fragility.
newsitem.headline: British manufacturing shows fresh fragility.

text.p: Britain's manufacturing sector slipped back in August, official figures showed, defying market forecasts and casting fresh doubt on the strength of the British economic recovery.
Manufacturing output fell 0.3 percent on the month and was 0.9 percent below its level a year ago. Economists had forecast a 0.4 percent increase in output.

"We had thought the stock mountain had been wound down quite significantly and we would begin to see the benefit of strong consumer spending cutting through to manufacturing output," said Stephen Hannah, head of research at IBJ International.
"It hasn't happened, the sector still looks quite weak."
Industrial production figures, which represent manufacturing and energy industry output and were also released by the Office for National Statistics on Monday, fell 0.4 percent in August.
In stark contrast to Monday's data, recent surveys from the Confederation of British Industry and Chartered Institute of Purchasing Supply have painted a bullish picture.
September's purchasing managers' index from the CIPS showed output and new order levels posted the largest monthly increases since the autumn of 1994, following a rise in output in August.
And the CBI's industrial trends surveys of the past three months have shown improving expectations for total output.

The UK Treasury pointed to the survey evidence and said the fall in official manufacturing output in August followed a healthy 0.6 percent rise in July. That added up to a manufacturing sector "on the up", a Treasury official said.

But economists said Monday's data cast doubt on the ability of British manufacturers' to tackle the twin millstones of weak European export markets and the mountains of unsold stocks, made a year ago and more when prospects looked brighter.
The Office for National Statistics itself said the trend in manufacturing was basically flat.
"Recent surveys have suggested a turnaround in this sector but so far they have proved rather wide of the mark," said Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident.

He said one month's figures did not require drastic action, in terms of fiscal or monetary policy. "But such data will certainly help the Chancellor resist any pressure for base rate increases in the autumn."

Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke will come under intense from his colleagues in the ruling Conservative Party to cut interest rates and taxes in the run-up to elections that must be held by May 1997.

A run of strong economic data in recent weeks, showing UK consumers spending fast, had prompted many City economists to call for an early tightening of monetary policy to choke off inflationary pressures.
But now it seems Britain's manufacturers are still ailing.
"Although demand is strengthening, firms are still able to meet if off the shelves, rather than stepping up new production," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.
He also said the newfound strength of the pound, up four percent on a trade-weighted basis in two months, posed further dangers to a manufacturing recovery which has barely begun.

"Export markets are crucial for the manufacturing sector and a further loss of competitiveness for UK firms, due to a further appreciation of the pound, could stifle any manufacturing recover before it really begins."
Loynes agreed the new slide in manufacturing fortunes meant Clarke would resist calls from the Bank of England to hike official interest rates to 6.00 percent, from 5.75 now.
"The figures offer confirmation that the gulf between consumers and industry remains wide....There is no chance that Mr Clarke will give in to Mr George's request for higher rates."
